description: We are competing in the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge at the NASA Space Apps Challenge! Unlike regular satellites that get blocked by clouds or darkness, Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) uses microwave pulses to see through anything and measure surface changes down to the centimeter. Our goal is to build an interactive, open-source web app using real NASA-ISRO (NISAR) radar data to visualize and analyze real-world changes on Earth—like shifting glaciers, deforestation, or earthquake fault line
summary:
Flooding can damage communities, agriculture, and infrastructure. Rapid identification of inundated areas is important for disaster response and planning. This project proposes a flood detection workflow using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery from the Sentinel-1 satellite. Unlike optical satellites, Sentinel-1 collects useful observations during day and night and is less affected by cloud cover, making it valuable during severe weather.

The project will compare Sentinel-1 images acquired before and after a flood event over a selected study area. The imagery will be preprocessed through radiometric calibration, speckle filtering, and terrain correction. Changes in radar backscatter will then be analysed to identify locations where water has likely inundated previously dry land. A threshold-based classification method will create a preliminary flood extent map. Where reference data are available, the results will be compared with reference maps or optical imagery to assess reliability.

Expected outputs include processed SAR images, a flood extent map, and an estimate of the affected area. The project demonstrates how Earth observation and remote sensing can support flood monitoring and disaster management. It also highlights limitations such as radar shadow, urban surfaces, vegetation, and confusion with permanent water bodies. It can also help authorities prioritize emergency response and relief.
details: This project focuses on detecting and mapping flood-affected areas using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite imagery from the Sentinel-1 satellite. It works by comparing satellite images captured before and after a flood event to identify changes in water coverage and detect flooded regions. SAR technology uses microwave signals, allowing it to collect useful data during cloudy weather and at night. The satellite images are processed using techniques such as speckle filtering, backscatter analysis, and threshold-based classification to distinguish flooded areas from non-flooded regions. The project uses Python as the programming language, Google Earth Engine and Google Colab for satellite data processing, and libraries such as NumPy, Matplotlib, Rasterio, and Geemap for analysis and visualization. QGIS can also be used to view and analyse the generated flood maps. The major benefits of this project include faster flood detection, monitoring of affected agricultural and residential areas, and the use of freely available satellite data. Its intended impact is to support disaster management authorities, emergency response teams, and local communities by providing useful information for rescue operations and relief planning. The creative aspect of this project is the application of AI and remote sensing techniques to identify flooded areas using radar imagery instead of relying only on optical satellite images. Factors such as image quality, spatial resolution, terrain conditions, vegetation, permanent water bodies, urban structures, classification accuracy, and data availability are considered to improve the reliability of the results.
